doc.title: Josiah Gluck interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 13, 2022

title: Technology serving the music; art of recording; mix as personal taste
summary: He sees technology and music as a collaboration, says the best recordings hide the technology, and discusses genre dictating the mix and letting band members ride their own faders.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: I know well you know it’s a funny instrument, it’s a funny word, it’s got the hard k sound you know, comedy. What can I tell you? But yeah I like to think that the technology and the music are — it should be a collaboration and a cooperation of how you’re getting this done, which is the same way I’ve always felt that the phrase when they talk about so-and- so you know Intergalactic Records recording artist and so forth, yes, because there is an art to making a recording. And there are some people who are great players, they’re not necessarily great performers, but there is an art to making a recording and knowing how to use the studio and help put things forward. And one of the things I’ve talked about at Peabody and a couple of other things is you know all of this gear you can put up on a bench, on a test bench, and prove in a very precise manner how well it does its job: frequency response, rise time of this, phase lock of that, all of these things you can really measure how precisely it works. But we use it to capture and manipulate, re-convey that art form which to me is the most personal in that we can all look at a Picasso or a Renoir or a Michelangelo and say, “Well this is blue, this is green, this is this form, this is that form. But music is that sort of thing that affects all of us very personally, very deeply. This is the way I feel about it. And you know I like something that you like — seriously? And vice versa. And so you take that very personal, very almost intimate way you experience it and yet you have to use all of this precise technology to capture it and then re-convey it. And I just think that that’s a very interesting marriage of two things. It’s — you know I like to say that theory and my Metrocard will get me on the subway but nonetheless it’s just an interesting way of looking at it and so forth. And the most successful recordings to me are the ones, and I always look at some of The Beatles and other things, where just somehow all of the technology just sort of recedes into the background and all you are left with is the music. That you’re not aware of things. Like certain film directors have that kind of where they’re right in your face, “Oh look at me, I’m being directed. I’m directing the movie.” And I feel certain record producers can be, “Look at me I’m producing.” But the things that just sort of leave you with the experience of the music and the sound and everything serves it and nothing is overly
flashy or distracting. Those to me are the — and how do you really define it? It’s like well it’s a mystery. But I mean it’s the sort of thing when things work you just know it.

That makes me think what you said about 15 minutes ago when the musicians came in and they didn’t tell you they needed more of this or more of that, sort of that thing you’ve achieved, recording karma or something.

Well it’s like when I said earlier about you know this is that and then this is personal taste on either side you know. It’s a question of if your taste and your sensibilities match what other people like. But also if you listen to certain records — yeah if I’m doing a little jazz trio or quartet or something with a singer, that kind of, that music, that genre kind of dictates how the mix’s already going to be. You kind of have a starting point which is half the history of recorded sound. But if you’re doing like the Fine Young Cannibals that you mentioned, that’s new, that’s different, and I think it’s a question of what can we get away with and what can we make ourselves — how you make things stand out. I mean don’t forget that thing, if it’s playing on the Muzak somewhere kind of at low level, you’ll still hear that. You’ll know what that is instantly. So that sonic branding is I think as equally as important as taking the dictation and being true to the music. And yeah there are times at SNL where things are really out there and things which are much more traditional. And there are certain bands where there are very complex things where all these different synths or people coming in with a big band like an Arcade Fire or something like that, I welcome the direction because, or if someone says, “Well I need this little echo move right here and this verb thing.” I’ll be like, “Guess what? This is your fader, it’s live TV, you’re out with these guys 739 nights a year, you know where this move is, this is your fader, good-bye and good luck. You do it.” It also gets them involved in it and so forth and because there are certain people who’ll just be sit there don’t even look at my console, don’t touch my console and all of that. And I don’t know I just don’t understand any reason why you would do that. It just makes no sense to me why you wouldn’t want the help.
